title: Thomas-Fermi screening of electrostatic fields in a type-I superconductor
authors: Nikhil Seeja Sivakumar, Tyler James, Frederick Carlisle, Philip Moriarty, Brian Kiraly
abstract: The empirical London equations make distinct predictions for a superconductor's longitudinal and transverse electrodynamic response. Conventionally, this framework attributes the Meissner effect to the transverse component, with the longitudinal response predicted to remain unchanged on entering the superconducting state, i.e. a static electric field is screened over the Thomas-Fermi length ($λ_{\mathrm{TF}} \sim 1$~Å), just as in the nonsupercondcuting metal. J.~E.~Hirsch~[\textit{Phys.~ Rev.~B}~\textbf{69},~214515~(2004)] has developed an alternative formalism, which predicts that the longitudinal screening length should instead be governed by the London penetration depth as the system is cooled below the superconducting transition temperature ($T_{\mathrm{c}}$). Here we use a combination of qPlus atomic force microscopy and scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy of single-crystal Pb(111) at $\sim$~340~mK~ \mbox{($T/T_{\mathrm{c}}\sim0.05$)} in an attempt to detect any modifications in electrostatic screening of the longitudinal tip field upon entering the superconducting phase. We quench superconductivity using a magnetic field of 200 mT normal to the Pb(111) surface. By measuring force-distance curves and local field-emission resonance spectra at the same sample position in the presence and absence of the magnetic field, we constrain the change in screening between the normal and superconducting state to less than $\sim 1 \%$. This is between two to three orders of magnitude smaller than that predicted by Hirsch's theory, and entirely consistent with unmodified Thomas-Fermi screening across the superconducting transition.
summary: This experimental study investigates whether the electrostatic screening of a superconductor changes upon entering the superconducting state. Using advanced AFM and STM techniques on Pb(111), the authors measured the force-gradient and local electronic density of states in both normal and superconducting states. The results strongly constrain any change in screening to be negligible, supporting the view that the Meissner effect is primarily a transverse electrodynamic phenomenon.
main_problem: The study aims to experimentally detect any modification in the electrostatic screening of longitudinal electric fields when a type-I superconductor enters the superconducting state.
main_result: The measurements constrain the change in screening to be significantly smaller than theoretical predictions, suggesting that the electrostatic screening remains consistent with unmodified Thomas-Fermi screening across the superconducting transition.
method: The research combines qPlus atomic force microscopy (AFM) and scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy (STM/STS) measurements on single-crystal Pb(111).
model_or_system: The physical system is the Pb(111) surface studied at very low temperatures ($T/T_c \sim 0.05$). Theoretical models compared include the traditional London equations and Hirsch's alternative formalism regarding longitudinal screening lengths.
key_observables: Electrostatic screening measured via frequency-shift ($\Delta f(z)$) curves (AFM) and resonance energy shifts ($\Delta V_p$) in Field Emission Resonance (FER) spectroscopy (STM).
important_parameters: Temperature ($T/T_c \sim 0.05$), magnetic field ($B=200 	ext{ mT}$), screening lengths ($\lambda_{TF}$ vs. $\lambda_L$), and quantitative limits (e.g., $< 1\%$ change, $< 0.17 	ext{ Hz}$ uncertainty).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the simple dipole-dipole interaction model for interpreting AFM results, and the use of a one-dimensional image-potential model for FER analysis.
figures_summary: Figures show comparisons of $\Delta f(z)$ curves between superconducting and normal states, and FER spectra comparing measurements taken with and without an applied magnetic field, consistently showing no detectable change.
paper_structure: The paper develops the problem by contrasting theoretical predictions (London vs. Hirsch) and then presents experimental evidence using both AFM and STM/STS techniques to test these predictions on Pb(111).
why_interesting: While focused on superconductivity, the use of highly sensitive local probes (AFM/STM) to measure fundamental electrostatics at the nanoscale provides insights into boundary conditions and screening mechanisms relevant to quantum interfaces.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
